stories.title: How Thailand’s Limestone Islands Formed
stories.subtitle: From an ancient seabed to the dramatic towers of Phang Nga Bay
stories.description: Discover how ancient sea sediments became limestone, how rainwater carved tall rock towers, and why those towers now rise from the sea. Practise useful English with Armenian vocabulary support, reading questions, and speaking prompts.

media.alt: Ko Tapu limestone sea stack surrounded by the green waters and cliffs of Phang Nga Bay, Thailand.
media.caption: The limestone towers of Phang Nga Bay began as sediments beneath an ancient sea.
media.changes: Wikimedia thumbnail; displayed with responsive cropping.

media.alt: A steep, vegetation-covered limestone tower rises from the sea in Phang Nga Bay.
media.caption: Water gradually widened cracks and removed surrounding limestone, leaving steep towers.
media.changes: Wikimedia thumbnail; displayed responsively.

stories.title: Maya Bay: Stone, Cinema, and a Second Chance
stories.subtitle: An illustrated journey through ancient limestone, a famous film, a living sea, and the work of recovery.
stories.description: Explore the complete story of Maya Bay: its ancient cliffs, turquoise water, people and film history, the 2018 closure, the latest 2026 conservation evidence, and how to visit thoughtfully. Includes five real photographs, two maps, a geology diagram, and a full English lesson with Armenian vocabulary.

media.alt: Turquoise water at Maya Bay framed by steep green limestone cliffs and coastal vegetation in March 2026.
media.caption: Maya Bay photographed on 17 March 2026. The limestone walls frame a real opening to the Andaman Sea.
media.changes: Wikimedia-generated 960-pixel thumbnail; no content alteration.

media.alt: White sand and translucent shallow water in Maya Bay, with boats near the rocky opening, photographed in 2007.
media.caption: White sand and shallow water at Maya Bay, 2 March 2007. This historical photograph predates the 2018 closure and later visitor rules.
media.changes: Wikimedia-generated 1280-pixel thumbnail; no content alteration.

media.alt: A 2017 view from beneath a rock overhang showing many boats in Maya Bay.
media.caption: Boats in Maya Bay on 11 June 2017, before the 2018 closure. The image records an earlier pattern of tourism, not current access arrangements.
media.changes: Wikimedia-generated 1280-pixel thumbnail; no content alteration.

media.alt: Steep weathered limestone cliffs above the pale beach and blue-green water of Maya Bay.
media.caption: The limestone walls and pale beach of Maya Bay, photographed on 11 March 2007. The rock is far older than the present shoreline.
media.changes: Wikimedia-generated 960-pixel thumbnail; no content alteration.

media.alt: Boats inside Pileh Lagoon among tall green limestone walls, photographed in 2018.
media.caption: Pileh Lagoon on Phi Phi Leh, 6 June 2018. This is a different inlet from Maya Bay; the two places are often included in the same island excursion.
media.changes: Wikimedia-generated 960-pixel thumbnail; no content alteration.

media.alt: Regional map placing Maya Bay on Phi Phi Leh southeast of Phuket and south of Krabi, with separate markers for Phi Phi Don, Karon, Phuket Town, Ao Nang and Krabi Town.
media.caption: Maya Bay in its regional setting. Coastlines use Natural Earth data; place markers are approximate. This orientation map is not for navigation.

media.caption: Different bays on one island. The actual island outline and named feature positions come from OpenStreetMap. Orientation only; check permitted access with park staff.

stories.title: Phi Phi Islands: A Story Written in Stone and Sea
stories.subtitle: Ancient cliffs, island lives, living reefs, and the patient work of protecting a remarkable place.
stories.description: Explore Phi Phi through a complete illustrated story: all six islands, limestone and karst, local maritime heritage, Viking Cave, coral reefs, the 2004 tsunami, and Maya Bay’s conservation journey. Includes maps, credited photographs, Armenian vocabulary, grammar, and speaking practice.

media.alt: View from the hillside over Phi Phi Don, with two curved bays separated by a narrow inhabited strip of land.
media.caption: Phi Phi Don from its eastern viewpoint, photographed in March 2010. The narrow low-lying strip between Ton Sai Bay and Loh Dalum Bay connects the island’s larger limestone masses.
media.credit: Amitparikh / Wikimedia Commons — Public domain (released by the photographer)
media.changes: Downloaded the existing Wikimedia thumbnail; no content edits.

media.alt: Four labelled scientific cross sections show marine carbonate sediments becoming limestone, tectonic uplift and fracturing, water dissolving cracks into caves and karst, and sea-level change and coastal erosion shaping islands.
media.caption: A simplified model for Phi Phi’s limestone cliffs. The rock formed long before the present coastline; tectonics, dissolution, sea-level change and erosion overlap in time. Conceptual cross sections, not to scale. Phi Phi also contains other rock types.

media.alt: Towering wooded limestone cliffs around the dark blue water and small boats at Pileh Lagoon on Phi Phi Leh.

stories.title: Ko Panyi: A Village Between Stone and Sea
stories.subtitle: The people, limestone, faith, football, and everyday ingenuity of Thailand’s remarkable village on stilts
stories.description: Explore Ko Panyi in depth: its limestone setting, remembered founders, Thai Muslim community, stilt architecture, school, fishing economy, football story, and changing future. Includes real credited photographs, two maps, an explanatory diagram, Armenian vocabulary support, grammar, exercises, and speaking practice.

stories.title: James Bond Island: The Stone, the Sea and the Story
stories.subtitle: A complete journey through Khao Phing Kan, Ko Tapu and the living world of Phang Nga Bay.
stories.description: Explore the real places behind James Bond Island: ancient limestone, a famous 1974 film, local legends, mangroves, caves and coastal communities. A detailed illustrated English lesson with original maps, Armenian vocabulary, grammar and speaking practice.
stories.excerpt: The famous pillar is only the beginning. Discover the stone, the cinema and the living bay around it.

media.alt: Ko Tapu rises from green water between larger limestone islands, with a small boat at the left.
media.caption: Ko Tapu, the distinctive limestone pillar beside Khao Phing Kan. Photograph taken in 2007.
media.changes: Wikimedia 1280-pixel rendition; downloaded without further alteration.

media.alt: Regional map of southern Thailand showing James Bond Island northeast of Phuket, Ko Panyi to its north, Khao Lak farther northwest, Krabi to the east and the separate Phi Phi Islands to the south.
media.caption: Where the story takes place: James Bond Island is in Phang Nga Bay. Coastline is based on Natural Earth; landmark positions are approximate. This is an orientation map, not a navigation chart.
media.credit: Story Atlas — original cartography; coastline from Natural Earth (public domain)
media.license: Original map created for Story Atlas; Natural Earth base data public domain
media.changes: Original regional map drawn from clipped public-domain Natural Earth coastline data; labels and approximate geographic landmark markers added.

media.alt: Schematic map, not to scale, showing western and eastern hills of Khao Phing Kan connected by a sandy tombolo, Ko Tapu in the northern cove, and the leaning slab at the western hill.
media.caption: Read the local geography: Khao Phing Kan includes two hills joined by sand; Ko Tapu is a separate sea stack offshore. Original schematic, not to scale, based on the Thai Department of Mineral Resources description.
media.license: Original illustration created for Story Atlas
media.changes: New schematic illustration; no source image copied. Shapes and distances are deliberately simplified, not to scale.

media.alt: Four-panel original geology diagram explains marine sediments becoming limestone, uplift and fractures, rainwater dissolution forming karst, and water surrounding eroded limestone remnants.
media.caption: How a seabed becomes a karst landscape. These processes overlap and recur; this diagram does not assign the present shape of Ko Tapu the much older age of its limestone.
media.license: Original illustration created for Story Atlas
media.changes: New explanatory diagram based on geological processes; no source image copied. All panels are schematic.

media.alt: Aerial view of Phang Nga Bay with forested limestone hills, tidal channels and dense mangroves.
media.caption: Phang Nga Bay seen from above: limestone hills, tidal channels and mangrove forest form one connected landscape. Photograph taken in 2017.
media.changes: Wikimedia 1280-pixel rendition; downloaded without further alteration.

media.alt: Visitors stand beneath a huge sloping limestone slab beside a dark recess at Khao Phing Kan.
media.caption: The leaning rock at Khao Phing Kan gives the larger island its own identity, beyond the famous offshore pillar. Photograph taken in 2019.
media.changes: Wikimedia 1280-pixel rendition; downloaded without further alteration.

media.alt: Close view of the Ko Tapu pillar, showing its narrow dark base, rough limestone walls and plants near the top.
media.caption: A closer view of Ko Tapu reveals its narrow base, irregular rock surface and patches of vegetation. The Commons record does not provide a confirmed capture date.
media.changes: Wikimedia 960-pixel-wide rendition; downloaded without further alteration.

media.alt: Waterside buildings on stilts and wooden boats at Ko Panyi, backed by a forested limestone cliff.
media.caption: Ko Panyi is a separate village in Phang Nga Bay, often visited on a wider bay excursion. This archival photograph was taken in 2004.
